notes: Lesson on organisation of the periodic table. Structure: hook (Mendeleev story) → table overview diagram → periods and groups → metals/nonmetals/metalloids → element symbol/number/mass → video → periodic trends → practice.

units.label: Title: The Periodic Table of Elements
Hook: Mendeleev's arrangement (text)
units.content_summary: Dmitri Mendeleev (1869) arranged 63 known elements by atomic mass and noticed repeating patterns. He left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties — later confirmed. The modern periodic table is arranged by atomic number.

units.label: Learning Objectives (text)
units.content_summary: Objectives: describe how the periodic table is organised; distinguish periods and groups; identify metals, nonmetals, metalloids; read element symbol, atomic number, atomic mass from a cell.

units.label: Periodic table full diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Full colour periodic table showing all 118 elements. Colour-coded by category (alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, transition metals, nonmetals, halogens, noble gases, metalloids). Periods and groups numbered.

units.label: Reading a periodic table cell (image)
units.content_summary: Magnified view of a single periodic table cell (e.g. Carbon): atomic number (6) at top, element symbol (C) in centre, element name (Carbon) below, atomic mass (12.011) at bottom.

units.label: Atomic number and mass explanation (text)
units.content_summary: Atomic number = number of protons (defines the element). Atomic mass = weighted average of all isotopes' masses. Elements arranged by increasing atomic number (not atomic mass, unlike Mendeleev's original table).

units.label: Periods: horizontal rows (text)
units.content_summary: Periods are the 7 horizontal rows. Period number = number of electron shells. Going across a period, atomic number increases by 1 each element. Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells but different numbers of electrons.

units.label: Groups: vertical columns (text)
units.content_summary: Groups (families) are the 18 vertical columns. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties. Group 1 = alkali metals (very reactive); Group 18 = noble gases (very unreactive).

units.label: Metals, nonmetals, metalloids diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Periodic table with staircase line separating metals (left, including transition metals) from nonmetals (right) and metalloids (along staircase: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, Po). Each category shaded differently.

units.label: Metals properties (text)
units.content_summary: Metals: shiny lustre, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable (can be hammered), ductile (can be drawn into wire), solid at room temperature (except mercury). ~80% of elements are metals.

units.label: Nonmetals properties (text)
units.content_summary: Nonmetals: dull or colourful appearance, poor conductors (insulators), brittle when solid, exist as solids, liquids, or gases at room temperature. Examples: carbon (C), nitrogen (N), oxygen (O), sulfur (S), chlorine (Cl).

units.label: Metalloids properties (text)
units.content_summary: Metalloids (semimetals): properties intermediate between metals and nonmetals. Examples: silicon (Si), germanium (Ge). Semiconductors used in electronics (computer chips). Silicon is the basis of the semiconductor industry.

units.label: Video: tour of the periodic table (video)
units.content_summary: Animated 3-minute tour highlighting key groups: alkali metals (explosive with water), halogens (highly reactive), noble gases (inert), transition metals (colourful compounds). Shows real element samples and their reactions.

units.label: Periodic trends overview (text)
units.content_summary: Brief introduction to trends: atomic radius decreases across a period, increases down a group. Electronegativity increases across a period. Ionisation energy increases across a period. These trends arise from nuclear charge and electron shell effects.

units.label: Practice: reading the periodic table (text)
units.content_summary: Six practice questions: identify element from atomic number; give group and period for specified elements; classify as metal/nonmetal/metalloid; explain why noble gases are unreactive; predict properties of an unknown element based on its position.
